body.x: Visual inspection on a factory line requires imaging conditions and inspection criteria matched to each product's shape, material and surface characteristics. Conventional inspection systems are often built for specific products, so equipment and inspection criteria must be adjusted whenever production changes.

A.I.Matics, an AI image recognition company led by CEO Hoon Lee, took a software-based approach to the problem with AIM-T1, an AI vision inspection platform. The company recently announced that AIM-T1 won CES 2027 Innovation Awards in two categories: Artificial Intelligence and Construction & Industrial Tech.

The CES Innovation Awards are presented by the Consumer Technology Association (CTA) ahead of CES, the world's largest IT and consumer electronics show, based on an overall evaluation of technology, design and innovation. CES 2027 is scheduled for January 2027 in Las Vegas.

AIM-T1 combines modular hardware with inspection software. When production shifts to a different product, inspection criteria can be updated through software. The platform is designed to generate inspection models for new products using defect-free reference samples. The system combines in-context learning, which enables adaptation using reference examples, with world model technology.

On the hardware side, the optical unit uses a liquid lens and electronic focus stacking. Precise electronic focus control maintains image sharpness across products with different heights and surface characteristics. Field workers can set inspection conditions, check results and improve models through the dedicated software.

A.I.Matics began as an in-house venture at Hyundai Motor Company in 2000 and has since developed expertise in vehicle image recognition technology. Its proprietary AI engine, aimNet, runs in more than 520,000 vehicles. The company adapted that technology, made lightweight for vehicle environments, for manufacturing inspection equipment and unveiled AIM-T1 in April.

"Introducing a new product on a manufacturing line requires considerable time and expense to reconfigure inspection equipment and criteria," Lee said. "AIM-T1 shifts inspection from hardware-dependent systems to software-driven processes, allowing a single machine to handle a wider range of products." He added, "We will use this award to speed up our expansion into overseas markets, including North America."
A.I.Matics plans to present AIM-T1 at CES 2027 and meet manufacturers, automation equipment companies and distribution partners.
